From the Bridge

A Holiday Message from the CO

As we approach the end of another busy year at HMCS Tecumseh, I want to take this opportunity to recognize the dedication, professionalism, and enthusiasm of our Ship's Company.

November is a particularly meaningful month for all of us who serve. Remembrance Day provides an opportunity to honour those who have served before us, especially those who made the ultimate sacrifice. It also reminds us of the responsibilities we carry today, and of the importance of maintaining the traditions and values that connect generations of Canadian sailors.

Throughout the year, our members balance their naval commitments with civilian careers, education, families, and countless other responsibilities. Your continued commitment to service and contribution to the Naval Reserve is the foundation of HMCS Tecumseh's success. The strength of our unit comes from its people and their willingness to support one another, step forward when needed, and contribute in ways both visible and unseen. The character, professionalism, and camaraderie demonstrated by our members create a unit that feels like family and serves as a source of pride for all who wear its crest. Whether on parade nights, during training, at community events, or behind the scenes, your efforts help foster the unique culture, sense of belonging, and spirit of service that make Tecumseh such a special place. It is because of you that Tecumseh continues to thrive as both a naval unit and a community.

As we look ahead to the holiday season, I encourage everyone to take time to enjoy the company of family and friends, recharge, and celebrate the accomplishments of the past year. I also want to extend my appreciation to the families and loved ones whose support makes our service possible. I wish you and your loved ones a happy, safe, and restful holiday season. May the coming year bring good health, happiness, and continued success.

Finally, I am pleased to see The Voice Pipe returning as a forum for sharing our experiences, celebrating our people, and preserving the history of HMCS Tecumseh. I encourage everyone to contribute and help make it a lasting part of our unit's culture.

Thank you for your continued service and commitment. I look forward to what we will accomplish together in the coming year.

Cdr Anna Kocot, CD
Commanding Officer | HMCS Tecumseh

The Masthead

From the Editor

Welcome to the second issue of The Voice Pipe.

When we relaunched the newsletter in October, the goal was to bring back a familiar part of HMCS Tecumseh's history while giving today's Ship's Company a place to share their experiences, accomplishments and stories.

I'm pleased to see that we're beginning to accomplish exactly that.

This issue has a distinctly seasonal flavour. November is a time for remembrance, and we're fortunate to have a firsthand account of the commemorations at the Somme from S1 Kimberly Chavez. We also look at some of the traditions that bring sailors together during the holiday season, from the annual Holiday Dinner to that most Canadian of naval concoctions, Moose Milk.

Our historical features continue to connect today's Tecumseh with earlier generations, while our Get to Know… section introduces another member of the unit's leadership team.

What I find particularly encouraging is the growing participation from members of the Ship's Company. A newsletter shouldn't be the work of one person, nor should it simply be a collection of official announcements. The most interesting stories often come from the people who experienced them.

There is plenty of room in future issues for training experiences, deployments, personal accomplishments, photographs, historical discoveries and even the occasional bit of naval humour. You don't need to be a writer to contribute. Sometimes a photograph and a few sentences are all it takes to get a good story started.

As we approach the end of another year, I'd like to thank everyone who has contributed to The Voice Pipe, and particularly those who have helped bring it back to life.

I hope you enjoy this issue, and I look forward to seeing what stories we'll have to tell in the new year.

Capt Mike Mirtle, CD
Unit Historian | Editor, The Voice Pipe

Get to Know… Our XO

Meet the XO: LCdr Steve Charest, CD

Executive Officer, HMCS Tecumseh

Lieutenant-Commander Steve Charest currently serves as Executive Officer of HMCS Tecumseh and is a Personnel Selection Officer (PSO). With more than three decades of service in the Canadian Armed Forces, his career has taken him across the Regular Force, Army and Naval Reserves, aviation, recruiting, personnel selection, and leadership roles.

LCdr Charest joined the CAF on 15 May 1990 under the Regular Officer Training Plan and attended Royal Military College Saint-Jean. He graduated in 1995 with an Honours Bachelor of Arts in Military and Strategic Studies. Originally an Air Navigator, he completed his air navigation training in Winnipeg before qualifying as a Tactical Coordinator on the Sea King helicopter. He subsequently served on the West Coast, including significant time embarked aboard HMCS Huron.

In 2000, LCdr Charest moved to Toronto to work with the Air Cadet Program in Central Ontario, overseeing training delivery and program administration. After leaving the Regular Force in 2004, he joined the Primary Reserve in Calgary and spent several years as a Military Career Counsellor at the Canadian Forces Recruiting Centre Calgary. He later served with 41 Canadian Brigade Group in a variety of recruiting, outreach, personnel and G1 roles.

In 2014, LCdr Charest transferred to the Personnel Selection Officer occupation. Since then, his career has focused heavily on recruiting, personnel selection and career development. After serving with Canadian Forces Recruiting Group in the Prairies and North, he returned to the Primary Reserve and joined the Naval Reserve in 2019. Within NAVRES, he has served in several PSO roles, including as Regional PSO for Western Region and, at various times, supporting the Central and Eastern regions. He assumed the role of Executive Officer of HMCS Tecumseh in June 2024 and also contributes to NAVRES recruiting training and standards at the national level.

Priorities as Executive Officer

As XO, LCdr Charest has focused on three closely connected priorities: growth, meaningful training and retention. His aim has been to support the Commanding Officer’s priorities while helping make HMCS Tecumseh a unit where members genuinely want to serve.

“I want our members to look forward to coming to the unit, to have access to training that is both valuable and rewarding, and to see opportunities to grow and progress throughout their Naval Reserve careers. Recruiting people is important, but creating an environment where they want to stay, contribute and succeed is equally important.”

A Message to the Ship’s Company

As he enters his final year as Executive Officer, LCdr Charest remains particularly appreciative of the people who make up HMCS Tecumseh.

“I have thoroughly enjoyed my time as XO and, most importantly, the opportunity to interact with our sailors and officers. One of the most rewarding parts of the role has been seeing members develop, take on new challenges and progress in their careers. I am proud of what our Ship’s Company continues to accomplish, and I look forward to seeing that growth continue well into the future.”

Tecumseh: Then and Now

An Old Tradition, A Wider Welcome

From a New Year’s reception in 1962 to a broader welcome for Calgary.

The New Year’s Levee is one of Canada’s oldest traditions of hospitality, with the first recorded Canadian reception held in New France in 1646. Over the centuries, the custom found a lasting place in military messes, where guests gathered to exchange greetings, renew friendships and begin another year together.

At HMCS Tecumseh, the tradition has deep roots. The Crowsnest recorded a New Year’s Day open house in 1951, welcoming fellow service members, naval association members and prominent Calgarians. In 1953, both the wardroom and the Chief and Petty Officers’ Mess received friends of the Navy. A photograph published in February 1962 captured Commanding Officer Cdr A. R. Smith speaking with the Honourable Douglas S. Harkness, Minister of National Defence and MP for Calgary North, while LCdr V. E. Schooley looked on.

On 1 January 2025, Tecumseh took a new step by opening its annual Levee to the general public for the first time. Civilian guests had attended previous receptions, but this was a broader invitation to Calgary itself: an opportunity to meet the people of the Naval Reserve, discover the unit and share a familiar tradition. The photographs from 1962 and 2026 show that sense of welcome continuing, with conversation and camaraderie at the heart of the occasion.

Much has changed since 1962. The faces, uniforms and surroundings are different, but the purpose remains remarkably familiar: to greet the New Year, strengthen old connections and make room for new ones.

Unit Historian

Historical sources: The Crowsnest, February 1951; February 1953; February 1962; RAUSI / Calgary Herald, January 2025; Office of the Lieutenant Governor of Ontario, levée history.

Remembrance & Service

Remembering the Somme: 110 Years On

A journey of remembrance through France and Belgium by S1 Chavez.

This summer, I had the honour of representing the Canadian Armed Forces in France for the 110th anniversary of the Battle of the Somme. I travelled alongside CAF members from across the country, all of us united by the same purpose: to remember those who fell.

Our journey took us across the battlefields to the Caribou memorials, which honour the Newfoundland soldiers who fought and passed there. Standing at each one, on the same ground where so many young Canadians and Newfoundlanders were lost, gave the history a weight that no book could.

One of the most moving moments was the unveiling of the Danger Tree monument, a lasting marker of the place where so many soldiers fell and took cover from enemy fire. We then took part in the anniversary ceremony itself, marking 110 years since the battle began.

Our journey ended in Ypres, Belgium, at the Menin Gate, where we attended the Last Post ceremony. Held every evening, it honours the missing of the First World War. That night, the band of the Royal Newfoundland Regiment played, an honour given to very few bands. After standing at the Caribou memorials earlier in the trip, hearing them there made the moment even more meaningful. Being there as a Canadian soldier was a humbling way to close the journey.

Lest we forget.

S1 Kimberly Chavez
Story and photographs

Remembrance at Tecumseh

Music, Remembrance and the Field of Crosses

The people and music behind a Calgary tradition of remembrance.

Each November, Calgary’s Field of Crosses transforms a five-acre site into a place of remembrance. More than 3,700 white crosses commemorate Southern Albertans who died in military service. A separate display of 120 crosses honours the approximately 120,000 Canadians who have given their lives in service. The illuminated memorial remains visible day and night.

From 1 to 11 November, sunrise flag-raising and sunset flag-lowering ceremonies bring together Memorial Cross Families, serving members, choirs, pipers, buglers and the wider community. The Remembrance Day service on 11 November is a focal point, but the daily observances give people an opportunity to return, reflect and remember throughout the period.

HMCS Tecumseh has supported the Field of Crosses since its beginning. Over the years, the unit has taken part in well over 100 ceremonies, providing buglers and ceremonial attendance. Those contributions are sometimes brief, but they matter. A clear, solitary call can bring an entire gathering to silence and help give the ceremony its solemn rhythm.

For the musicians, a few notes may represent only a minute or two of a ceremony, yet they require practice, concentration and composure in the cold of an Alberta November.

The Field of Crosses began as a personal memorial initiative and has grown into a community-supported charitable undertaking. Its meaning rests not only in the crosses themselves, but also in the families, volunteers and service members who return year after year. Tecumseh’s continuing participation is part of that shared commitment to remembrance.

Customs & Traditions

A Holiday Tradition: When the Officers Serve the Crew

The Canadian military Holiday Dinner · history, gratitude and camaraderie

Few Canadian military customs express the relationship between leaders and their people as clearly as the annual Christmas or Holiday Dinner. For one meal, the usual routine is turned around: officers and senior non-commissioned members take their place behind the serving line, while junior members are invited to sit down and enjoy the occasion.

The gesture is simple, but its meaning has endured. It is an opportunity for leaders to thank the people whose daily work keeps a unit functioning, and a chance for everyone to share a meal outside the ordinary rhythm of training and operations.

Historical photographs show that the custom has been part of Canadian military life for generations. In December 1942, Group Captain J. Plan was photographed serving Corporal M. Demers of 425 Squadron. Another wartime image captures senior RCAF officers carving turkeys for their personnel. These are familiar scenes: the people who ordinarily give the orders are the ones carrying the plates.

Even during wartime, a holiday meal could provide a moment of normality and fellowship. The well-known photographs of Canadians celebrating Christmas at Ortona in 1943 are a powerful reminder that such occasions mattered especially when ordinary comforts were scarce.

At HMCS Tecumseh, the tradition remains part of the unit’s annual calendar. The language has evolved from the historical “Christmas Dinner” or “Men’s Christmas Dinner” to today’s more inclusive “Holiday Dinner,” but the purpose is familiar: recognition, fellowship and a welcome break from the normal routine.

Tecumseh’s next Holiday Dinner is scheduled for 9 December 2026. Its photographs and stories will belong to a future edition.

Unit Historian

Historical reading: DND, Origins of the Soldiers Dinner; RCAF, Holiday Traditions in the Royal Canadian Air Force (2019); Naval Museum of Halifax, Holiday Traditions in the Navy (2020).

Naval Trivia

Moose Milk: A Canadian Naval Tradition

An unlikely name, a mysterious history, and a recipe that everyone seems to make differently.

When I joined the Naval Reserve at HMCS Tecumseh in 1983, Moose Milk was already a well-established tradition. It seemed to have always been part of naval life. Nobody particularly questioned where it came from, but everybody had an opinion about how it should be made. More than forty years later, I found myself wondering how far back the tradition goes. The answer is not as straightforward as you might expect.

From Moose Blood to Moose Milk?

One account of Moose Milk’s origins takes us back to colonial Canada and the New Year’s receptions of New France. According to the story, imported wines sometimes suffered during the Atlantic crossing and were made more palatable with additional alcohol, spices and heat. The resulting drink was supposedly known as Le Sang du Caribou, or Moose Blood.

As the story goes, British influence brought whisky into the mixture, while goat’s milk, nutmeg and cinnamon eventually transformed it into something resembling today’s Moose Milk.

It’s an entertaining explanation, but the documentary evidence connecting those early refreshments to modern Moose Milk is thin. As with many good naval stories, it may have improved in the telling.

A Favourite of the Canadian Navy

Whatever its beginnings, Moose Milk found a comfortable home in the Royal Canadian Navy. In January 2010, CPO2 (later promoted to CPO1) Sean Neraasen of HMCS Malahat wrote in Lookout about the tradition’s association with naval New Year’s Levees and receptions aboard HMC ships and at shore establishments.

Sean and I served together during the 1980s, so finding his article was a pleasant surprise.

Another familiar name surfaced: CPO2 Mark Nelson, who wrote about naval holiday traditions in 2022. Mark and I trained together in 1984 and often found ourselves on the same coast during summer training.

His basic naval recipe called for rum and vanilla ice cream, with other ingredients varying by local taste. A perfectly reasonable recipe, though not quite the one I remember.

The Tecumseh Version

At Tecumseh in the 1980s, Moose Milk was usually prepared by members of the Chief and Petty Officers’ Mess for the annual Men’s Christmas Dinner, now known as the Holiday Dinner.

In my experience, only two ingredients were essential: dark rum and milk. Everything else was open to negotiation.

Ice cream was common, with the preferred variety depending on who made the batch. Kahlúa, vodka, Baileys Irish Cream and eggnog were also popular additions. I don’t recall anyone consulting an official recipe, and precise measurements were not always a priority. Nutmeg was optional early on, but by the end of the 1980s it was becoming something of a required ingredient.

I also remember Moose Milk aboard HMCS Porte de la Reine, one of the three West Coast Gate Vessels used extensively for Naval Reserve training. Reservists sometimes crewed these vessels on holiday-period training cruises, and Moose Milk was part of the experience.

A Recipe for Tradition

One of the more interesting discoveries is just how many Moose Milk recipes exist across the Canadian Armed Forces. The Navy has its versions, the Army and Air Force theirs, and individual ships and messes have developed variations of their own. Some favour rum, others whisky; some use vanilla ice cream, while others rely on chocolate milk, cream or eggnog.

Finding the one authentic recipe may be hopeless.

Perhaps that’s because Moose Milk was never really about following instructions. It was about who made it, the occasion, and the shipmates who gathered to enjoy it.

Its precise origins may remain a mystery, but I can attest that the tradition was alive and well at HMCS Tecumseh more than forty years ago. Judging by the number of former shipmates who still have Moose Milk stories, it made quite an impression.

For those interested in continuing the tradition, we’ve included a few recipes in this issue’s From the Galley.

Unit Historian

Historical sources: CPO2 (later promoted to CPO1) Sean Neraasen, “The Tradition of Moose Milk and the Canadian Navy,” Lookout (2010); CPO2 (Ret’d) Mark Nelson, “Jackspeak: Holiday Traditions,” Pacific Navy News (2022); Maritime Engineering Journal, No. 68 (2011), review of The History of HMCS Bytown Wardroom Mess.
Personal recollections are the author’s own.

From the Galley

Moose Milk — A Naval Favourite

A traditional mess-sized recipe, with a few variations from across the Navy.

Traditional Naval-Style Moose Milk

There is no single official RCN formula, but this published version combines familiar ingredients: milk, vanilla ice cream, dark rum and coffee liqueur. It makes a substantial batch for a gathering.

Ingredients

  • 3 litres milk
  • 3 litres vanilla ice cream
  • 3 tablespoons vanilla
  • 350 mL coffee liqueur
  • 350 mL brandy
  • 1.25 litres dark rum
  • 1 litre cubed ice

Method: Combine half the ingredients in a large food-safe container and stir for five minutes. Add the remainder and stir for another five minutes. Serve chilled.

Original recipe and context: Pacific Navy News — HMCS VANCOUVER’s Moose Milk.

Every mess seems to have its own interpretation. Here are a few more worth exploring:

  • HMCS VANCOUVER’s version — a richer variation featuring chocolate, butterscotch and peanut butter.
  • HMCS IROQUOIS (2013) — a recipe shared during a visit to Liverpool, including rum, coffee liqueur and nutmeg.
  • Hamilton Naval Association — another traditional large-batch recipe.
  • Alcohol-free Moose Milk — a variation using ice cream, milk, rum extract, coffee and nutmeg.

Have a favourite Moose Milk recipe? Send it in for a future edition of The Voice Pipe. A family variation, a galley memory or a recipe with a naval connection would all be welcome.

Alcoholic recipes are intended for adults of legal drinking age; serve responsibly and offer an alcohol-free option.

Your Voice Pipe

Have a Story to Tell?

The history of Tecumseh has always been written, in part, by its own people. We invite today's ship's company to contribute news, photographs, training experiences, professional achievements, personal stories, historical finds, humour and favourite recipes.

You do not need to write a polished article. A few notes, a photograph with a caption, or an idea for a story can be a useful starting point.

Have something to contribute? Contact the Unit Historian about a story, photograph, historical item or recipe for a future issue: Capt Mike Mirtle <michael.mirtle@ecn.forces.gc.ca>

A Note About Public Distribution

The Voice Pipe is published online at voicepipe.ca and is freely accessible to the public. By submitting material for consideration, contributors acknowledge that approved articles and photographs may be published and shared publicly.

Please ensure submissions contain no sensitive or restricted information and that appropriate permission has been obtained to share photographs and other material.

All submissions are subject to editorial review and approval before publication.
